newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU has mixed success in narrowing wealth gap.
newsitem.headline: EU has mixed success in narrowing wealth gap.

text.p: Ten years of EU efforts to bridge the gap between its richest and poorest citizens have shown mixed success, with improvements at national level contrasting with growing wealth gaps at the regional and local levels.
"Disparities in income per head between member states have narrowed significantly (since 1983)," said a European Commission regional aid report released on Wednesday.
But at a lower level, the picture was less bright.
"Over the past decade, regional income disparities widened in all member states in which they are measured, with the exception of the Netherlands," the report said.
"Similarly, regional differences in unemployment rates also increased within many member states, with the UK as a notable exception," said the report on aid to the EU's 15 countries.

The mixed success is despite massive spending, past and planned, at more than six times the rate seen during the 1948-1951, U.S.-funded Marshall Plan to repair Europe after the ravages of World War Two fighting.
Money spent or earmarked by the bloc for 1989-1999 amounts to an annual 6.5 percent of countries' total output, dwarfing the annual one percent figure spent by the United States.
Between 1989 and 1993, the bloc spent 63 billion European currency units (Ecus) at 1995 prices ($79 billion) mainly trying to boost economic performance in the then 12 countries' poorest regions.
Money was also targeted on industrially declining regions -- so-called rust belts -- rural and sparsely populated areas, retraining, unemployment and farm and fisheries reform.
For the period from 1994 to 1999, with the new EU entrants Austria, Finland and Sweden on board, the EU plans to spend 170 billion Ecus on similar projects.
Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain -- the EU's poorest in terms of income per head -- moved from a collective two-thirds of the EU average in 1983 to nearly three-quarters in 1995.

Behind the headline improvement, Greece moved from 61.9 percent of the EU average to 64.3 percent, Ireland from 63.6 percent to 89.9, Spain from 70.5 to 76.2 percent and Portugal from 55.1 to 68.4 percent.
European Regional Aid Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies denied that widening disparities meant policies had failed.
"European structural policy cannot achieve the miracles which member states cannot achieve with much higher levels of funding," she told a news conference.

"What Europe has achieved and what's important...is that structural fund action in the European Union has been directed at investment, not only in infrastructure but also in small and medium-sized enterprises," she added. ($=0.79 Ecus)
